title: Stories and Explanations
bigQuestion: How do you make a true thing come alive on the page, whether it is a moment or a fact?

story.title: The Snow Day, Twice
story.kicker: Theo writes about a snow day. The first draft is true. The second draft is true and alive.
paragraphs: In January a storm dropped eleven inches of snow on Chicago, and school closed. On Monday, Ms. Okafor asked her fourth graders to write a true story about the snow day. Theo wrote fast. "I woke up. It was a snow day. I played outside with my brother. It was fun. Then I came in and had hot chocolate. The end."

Ms. Okafor read it and said, "Every word of this is true. And I cannot see any of it." Theo looked at the page. She was right. It could have been anyone's snow day. "Pick one part," she said. "The smallest part that mattered. Then slow down and show me."

Theo picked the moment the snow fort fell in. He closed his eyes and remembered. The wall had been taller than his brother, Eli. Eli had pushed one more block onto the top. There had been a soft whump, and then Eli's boots sticking out of a white pile, and Eli's muffled voice: "I'm okay! I'm okay!"

His second draft started in the middle of the action. "Eli lifted the last block over his head. 'Don't,' I said. He did." He added the whump. He added the cold that got inside his gloves. He added what Eli's voice sounded like from under the snow. He ended with the two of them lying in the wreck of the fort, laughing so hard they could not stand up.
When Theo read it aloud, two kids laughed at the whump. Ms. Okafor taped both drafts to the wall side by side. "Same day," she said. "Same boy. One of these is a list. The other one is a story."
story.think: Theo's first draft was true. Why did his teacher say she could not see it? What did he change?

lessons.title: Pick One Small Moment
lessons.mainIdea: A strong true story zooms in on one small moment instead of listing a whole day.
reading: Theo's first draft covered a whole day in six sentences. Wake up, play, come in, drink cocoa. That is a *list*, and a list is not a story. A story needs a camera that stops and holds still. Ms. Okafor told him to find the smallest part that mattered. He found ten seconds: the fort falling in.

Writers call this a *small moment*. It is one event that took a few minutes, or even a few seconds. The bus pulling away without you. The moment your dog first saw snow. The second the cake fell over. Small moments make better stories because you can slow down and show every detail.

To find yours, start with a big memory. Then ask: what is the one part I would tell a friend first? That is the moment. Everything else is background. You can mention the rest in a sentence, but the moment gets the whole page.

words.d: one short event, a few seconds or minutes long, that a true story zooms in on
a story, true or made up, that tells events in order

look.title: Zoom In
look.text: Lena's big memory is her birthday. Inside it are smaller moments: blowing out the candles, opening a box that turned out to have a kitten in it, her grandma singing off key, the kitten hiding under the couch for an hour. Lena has to pick one.
look.prompt: Which small moment would you choose to write about? What could you show in it that a list would leave out?

check.q: Why was Theo's first draft a list instead of a story?
choices: It covered a whole day in six sentences with no details
check.why: A whole day in six sentences cannot slow down. A story needs to hold still on one moment.

check.q: What is a small moment?
choices: A story about a small person
The last sentence of a story
One short event you zoom in on
check.why: A small moment is one event that took a few minutes or seconds, told with detail.

check.q: How can you find your small moment inside a big memory?
choices: Ask what part you would tell a friend first
Write the whole day, then stop
check.why: The part you would tell first is the part that mattered. That is the moment to zoom in on.

lessons.title: A Beginning That Hooks
lessons.mainIdea: Start inside the action, with a line of talk, a sound or a picture, so the reader has to keep going.
reading: Compare two first lines. "I woke up. It was a snow day." And: "Eli lifted the last block over his head. 'Don't,' I said. He did." The first one could begin a thousand stories. The second one makes you ask what happens next. That pull is called a *hook*.

Three kinds of hooks work well for a small moment. Start with action: someone is already doing something. Start with talk: a line of *dialogue*, the words a person says. Start with a sound or a picture: "Whump. Then silence, then boots." Any of these drops the reader into the moment instead of walking them to it.

What does not work? Starting at the start of the day. Starting with "I am going to tell you about." Starting with the weather unless the weather is the story. Try this: write your moment, then cut the first two sentences. Often the real hook was hiding in sentence three.

words.d: an opening that grabs the reader and makes them want to keep reading
the words characters say, shown with quotation marks

look.title: Three Openings for One Moment
look.text: 1. It was a Saturday and I was at the pool with my cousin. 2. "Jump," my cousin said. "I'm counting to three." 3. The diving board bounced under my feet, and the water looked a mile away.
look.prompt: Which opening is the weakest hook? What do the other two do that it does not?

check.q: What is a hook?
choices: The last line of a story
An opening that makes the reader want to keep going
A line that explains the setting
check.why: A hook grabs the reader at the start. It makes them ask what happens next.

check.q: Which opening starts with dialogue?
choices: The board bounced under my feet.
check.why: Dialogue is the words a person says. "Jump," my cousin said, starts with talk.

check.q: What trick can help you find a better hook?
choices: Add a sentence about the weather
Start with "I am going to tell you about"
Cut the first two sentences and see what is left
check.why: The real hook is often in sentence three. Cutting the slow start reveals it.

lessons.title: Talk and the Five Senses
lessons.mainIdea: Dialogue and sensory details let the reader hear, see and feel the moment instead of being told about it.
reading: "It was fun" tells. "Eli's boots stuck out of the pile and his muffled voice said, 'I'm okay! I'm okay!'" shows. The difference is *detail*. Theo's second draft gave the reader things to hear, see and feel. Those are called *sensory details*: details that use the five senses of sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.

You do not need all five in every paragraph. Pick the two or three that were strongest in the moment. For the fort, it was sound (whump, muffled voice) and touch (cold inside the gloves). Ask yourself: what did I hear? What did my hands feel? What could I smell? Write the honest answer.

Dialogue is another way to show. When Eli says "I'm okay!" twice, we learn he is scared and also fine, and we learn it faster than if Theo explained it. Keep dialogue short and real. People do not give speeches in a snow fort. Two or three lines of talk in a small moment is usually plenty.

words.d: a detail that uses one of the five senses: sight, sound, touch, smell or taste
a small, specific piece of a picture, sound or feeling
letting the reader see and hear the moment instead of just naming the feeling

look.title: Sensory Details in Theo's Two Drafts
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from the story drafts described above
look.prompt: What do the numbers say about the difference between a list and a story?

check.q: Which sentence uses a sensory detail?
choices: The cold got inside my gloves.
check.why: Cold inside the gloves is a touch detail. The others tell without showing.

check.q: How many senses should you use in one paragraph?
choices: The two or three that were strongest in the moment
check.why: Pick the senses that were really strong in that moment. Forcing all five sounds fake.

check.q: What does Eli's "I'm okay! I'm okay!" show the reader?
choices: That Eli is angry at Theo
That Eli is scared but fine
That the fort is still standing
check.why: Short real dialogue shows feeling fast. Saying it twice shows he is shaken but not hurt.

lessons.title: An Ending That Satisfies
lessons.mainIdea: A good ending lands on the feeling of the moment; it does not just stop or say the end.
reading: Theo's first draft ended with "The end." His second ended with the brothers lying in the wreck of the fort, laughing too hard to stand up. The first ending stops. The second one *lands*. It leaves the reader with the feeling the whole story was building toward.

Three ways to land a small moment. End with a picture: the last thing you saw. End with a line of talk: the last thing someone said. End with a thought: what you knew or felt right then, in one honest sentence. "We never rebuilt the fort. We did not need to." Any of these gives the story a place to rest.

What to avoid. Do not race to bedtime: "Then we went in and ate and went to sleep." Do not explain the lesson: "And that is why you should listen to your brother." Trust the reader. If you showed the moment well, they already feel it. Stop one sentence sooner than you think you should.

words.d: the last part of a story, where it lands on a feeling, picture or thought
feeling complete and right, so the reader does not need more

look.title: Which Landing?
look.text: A story about a lost dog found in the rain. Three endings. A. Then we went home and had dinner and went to bed. The end. B. She was soaked, and she smelled terrible, and I did not let go of her all the way home. C. The lesson is that you should always keep your dog on a leash.
look.prompt: Which ending lands on the feeling? What is wrong with the other two?

check.q: What is the difference between an ending that stops and one that lands?
choices: A landing ending leaves the reader with the story's feeling
A stopping ending has more dialogue
check.why: A landing gives the reader a place to rest on the feeling. Stopping just quits.

check.q: Which is an ending that races to bedtime?
choices: I did not let go of her all the way home.
Then we ate and went to sleep. The end.
The fort was gone, and I did not mind.
check.why: Racing to bedtime skips past the moment to finish the day. It drains the feeling out.

check.q: Why should you not explain the lesson at the end?
choices: Lessons are not allowed in stories
The teacher will take points off
It makes the story too short
If you showed the moment well, the reader already feels it
check.why: Trust the reader. A well-shown moment carries its own meaning.

lessons.title: Introduce and Group the Facts
lessons.mainIdea: Informative writing opens by naming the topic, then puts related facts together in groups.
reading: A story shows one moment. An *informative* piece explains a topic so a reader learns something true. Both are true writing, but they work differently. The story slows down. The informative piece organizes. Its first job is to tell the reader the topic in a sentence or two: "Monarch butterflies fly thousands of miles every fall, and Illinois is on their road."

The second job is *grouping*. Imagine you have twelve facts about monarchs on sticky notes. Some are about the wings. Some are about the trip south. Some are about milkweed. Put the wing facts together, the trip facts together, the food facts together. Each group becomes a paragraph. A reader can follow three groups; a reader cannot follow twelve loose facts.

Order the groups so they make sense. Often it is what a thing is, then what it does, then why it matters. The introduction names the topic and hints at the groups: "Monarchs have amazing wings, make an incredible trip, and need one plant to survive." Now the reader knows the map before the trip.

words.d: writing that explains a topic and gives true facts
what a piece of writing is about
to put facts that belong together into one paragraph

look.title: Sort the Sticky Notes
look.text: Six facts about the Chicago River: it once flowed into Lake Michigan; engineers reversed it in 1900; it is dyed green on St. Patrick's Day; it flows through downtown; boats give tours on it; reversing it kept waste out of the drinking water.
look.prompt: Which facts belong together? What would you name each group?

check.q: What is the first job of an informative piece?
choices: Start with a hook of dialogue
check.why: Informative writing names its topic first so the reader knows what they are learning.

check.q: Why group facts?
choices: A reader can follow a few groups but not many loose facts
Because facts must be in alphabetical order
check.why: Grouping turns a pile of facts into paragraphs a reader can follow.

check.q: How does an informative piece differ from a small-moment story?
choices: It organizes facts instead of slowing down on one moment
check.why: Both can be true. The story zooms in; the informative piece organizes what the reader needs to learn.

lessons.title: Headings, Pictures and Definitions
lessons.mainIdea: Headings, pictures and defined words help a reader find and understand the facts.
reading: Open a true book about volcanoes. You do not read every page. You look at the *headings*, the short bold titles above each part, and jump to the one you want. When you write informative text, give your reader the same help. Each group of facts gets a heading that says what it is about: "The Long Trip South."

A picture with a *caption* can carry a fact faster than a paragraph. A map with an arrow from Illinois to Mexico shows the monarch's trip in one look. A labeled drawing of a wing shows the scales. Draw it or find it, then write a caption: one sentence that tells what the picture shows.

Every topic has words the reader might not know. Milkweed. Migration. Do not skip them and do not just use them. *Define* them: give the meaning in plain words the first time the word appears. "Monarchs migrate, which means they travel a long way when the seasons change." A defined word is a gift to a reader who was about to get lost.

words.d: a short bold title above a part of a text that says what the part is about
one sentence under a picture that tells what it shows
to give the meaning of a word in plain words

look.title: One Section With Its Helpers
look.text: Heading: One Plant to Live On. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, a tall plant with thick leaves and a milky sap. Without milkweed, a monarch cannot grow up. Illinois has more than a dozen kinds of milkweed. Caption under a drawing: A monarch caterpillar, striped yellow, black and white, on a milkweed leaf.
look.cite: Model section written for this lesson
look.prompt: Find the heading, the defined word and the caption. What does each one do for the reader?

check.q: What does a heading do?
choices: Tells what a part of the text is about so a reader can find it
check.why: Headings are signposts. They let a reader jump to the part they need.

check.q: What is a caption?
choices: One sentence that tells what a picture shows
check.why: A caption sits under a picture and explains it in one sentence.

check.q: Which sentence defines a word?
choices: Monarchs migrate, which means they travel far when seasons change.
check.why: Defining means giving the meaning in plain words. The second sentence explains what migrate means.

lessons.title: Writing a How-To
lessons.mainIdea: A how-to lists what you need, then gives numbered steps in the exact order a reader must do them.
reading: Try to make a paper airplane from these directions: "Fold it and throw it." You cannot. A *how-to* is informative writing that teaches a reader to do something, and it only works if the steps are complete and in order. Start with a title that says the job: "How to Make a Paper Airplane That Flies Straight."

Next comes a list of what you need: one sheet of paper, a flat table. Then the *steps*, numbered. Each step is one action, starting with a verb: "1. Fold the paper in half the long way. 2. Open it flat again." Words like first, next, then, after that and finally help the reader keep their place.

The test of a how-to is simple. Give it to someone who has never done the thing, and watch them. Where do they stop and ask? That step is missing something. Where do they do it wrong? That step is unclear. Fix those spots. A how-to is finished when a stranger can follow it without asking you anything.

words.d: writing that teaches a reader to do something step by step
one action in a how-to, done in order

look.title: Find the Missing Step
look.text: How to make a peanut butter sandwich. 1. Get two slices of bread. 2. Spread peanut butter on one slice. 3. Put the slices together. 4. Cut the sandwich in half. A reader stops at step 2 and asks, "With what?" Another reader ends up with the peanut butter on the outside.
look.prompt: What does step 2 leave out? What should step 3 say so the peanut butter ends up inside?

check.q: What comes right after the title in a how-to?
choices: A list of what you need
check.why: The reader needs to gather materials before starting the steps.

check.q: How should each step begin?
check.why: Steps are commands: fold, open, cut. Starting with the verb makes each action clear.

check.q: How do you test a how-to?
choices: Ask a friend if it looks nice
Watch someone who has never done it try to follow it
check.why: Where the stranger stops or goes wrong, the how-to needs a fix.

lessons.title: From Notes to Paragraph
lessons.mainIdea: Writing from research means turning notes in your own words into organized paragraphs, and saying where the facts came from.
reading: Priya wants to write about the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. She reads two books and a museum website. She does not copy sentences. She takes *notes* in her own words, short phrases on index cards: "started Oct 8, 1871." "burned about 3 days." "around 300 people died." "city rebuilt with brick and stone." Each card also says which book or site it came from.

Then she groups the cards, just like sticky notes. One pile: how it started and spread. One pile: what was lost. One pile: how the city rebuilt. Each pile becomes a paragraph. She turns each phrase into a full sentence in her own words. Because the notes were already hers, the paragraphs are hers too.

At the end she lists her *sources*, the places the facts came from. Two reasons. First, it is honest: those writers did the work of finding the facts. Second, a reader who wants more knows where to look. Even a short list, "Books I used," with titles and authors, does the job in fourth grade.

words.d: short phrases in your own words that record facts from a source
the book, website or person a fact came from
finding facts about a topic by reading and asking

look.title: Priya's Note Cards by Pile
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from Priya's imagined cards
look.prompt: Which paragraph will be longest? What should Priya do with the two cards that do not fit?

check.q: How should you take notes from a source?
choices: Short phrases in your own words
check.why: Notes in your own words keep the writing yours and are easy to turn into sentences later.

check.q: Why write down which source each note came from?
choices: So you can list your sources honestly at the end
So you can copy it later
check.why: Naming sources is honest and lets a reader find more.

check.q: What do the grouped piles of cards become?
check.why: Each pile is one group of related facts, and each group becomes a paragraph.

lessons.title: Writing About a Text With Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: When you write about a text, make a point and then prove it with words or details from the text itself.
reading: Suppose the question is "How does the tortoise feel at the start of the race?" You could answer "She feels confident." Good, but a reader might ask how you know. So you add the proof: "When the hare laughs at her, she does not argue. She just says, 'Let us race.'" That proof from the text is *evidence*.

The pattern has three parts. Make your point. Give the evidence, either a short quote in quotation marks or a detail in your own words. Then explain how the evidence proves the point: "Someone who is nervous would argue or back down. She does neither." Point, evidence, explain. Many teachers call it P-E-E.

Choose evidence that really fits. Not every detail proves every point. If your point is that the hare is careless, the fact that he is fast does not help. The fact that he naps in the middle of a race does. Pick the detail that makes your reader nod.

words.d: words or details from a text that prove a point about it
to copy a text's exact words and put them in quotation marks
to tell how the evidence proves the point

look.title: Point, Evidence, Explain
look.text: The hare is careless. In the middle of the race, he lies down under a tree and falls asleep. A runner who cared about winning would never stop to nap with the finish line still ahead.
look.cite: Model answer about the old tortoise-and-hare tale, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which sentence is the point? Which is the evidence? Which one explains?

check.q: What is evidence when you write about a text?
choices: Words or details from the text that prove your point
check.why: Evidence comes from inside the text. It is how you show a reader you are right.

check.q: What are the three parts of the pattern?
check.why: Make the point, give evidence from the text, then explain how the evidence proves it.

check.q: Your point is that the hare is careless. Which detail is the best evidence?
choices: The hare naps in the middle of the race.
The race is on a road.
check.why: Napping mid-race shows carelessness. Being fast does not prove anything about care.

lessons.title: Pacing and Transitions
lessons.mainIdea: Pacing is how fast a piece moves, and transition words carry the reader smoothly from one part to the next.
reading: Theo gave the fort's fall a whole paragraph and the walk home one sentence. That is *pacing*: choosing how much space each part gets. Slow down where the moment matters and speed up where it does not. In informative writing, pacing means giving the important group of facts the most room and the small one the least.

*Transitions* are the words that move a reader between parts. In a story, they handle time: a moment later, by the time we got inside, the next morning. In informative writing, they handle ideas: another reason, in addition, on the other hand, finally. A transition is a hand on the reader's back saying this way.

Read your draft and mark every place the scene, time or idea changes. Is there a transition there? If a reader could get lost, add one. If the transition is doing nothing, cut it. Then check pacing: is the best part the biggest part? If the boring part is longest, cut it down and give the room to the moment that matters.

words.d: how fast a piece of writing moves; how much space each part gets
a word or phrase that moves the reader from one part or idea to the next

look.title: Sentences Per Part in Theo's Second Draft
look.cite: Counted for this lesson from the draft described in the story
look.prompt: Where did Theo slow down? Where did he speed up? Why do those choices make sense?

check.q: What is pacing?
choices: How fast a piece moves and how much space each part gets
check.why: Pacing is about space and speed. Slow down where it matters, speed up where it does not.

check.q: Which is a transition that handles time in a story?
check.why: The next morning moves the reader forward in time. The others move between ideas.

check.q: Your draft's longest part is the boring part. What should you do?
choices: Add more to the boring part
Cut it down and give the room to the part that matters
check.why: Good pacing gives the most space to the moment or facts that matter most.

choices: A story about a whole week
One short event a story zooms in on
review.why: A small moment is a few minutes or seconds, told with enough detail that the reader can see it.

review.q: Which opening is the strongest hook?
choices: I am going to tell you about my snow day.
I woke up and got dressed.
review.why: Starting inside the action with a line of talk pulls the reader in.

review.q: Which sentence shows instead of tells?
choices: The hallway was dark and my sneakers squeaked with every step.
review.why: Sensory details, dark and squeaking sneakers, let the reader feel the fear without being told.

choices: Then we ate dinner and went to sleep. The end.
I did not let go of her all the way home.
The fort was gone, and I did not mind.
review.why: Rushing to the end of the day drains the feeling. A good ending lands on the moment.

review.q: What is the second job of informative writing, after naming the topic?
review.why: Grouping turns a pile of facts into paragraphs a reader can follow.

choices: Tells what a picture shows in one sentence
review.why: A caption sits under a picture and explains what it shows.

review.q: In writing about a text, what comes after the point and the evidence?
choices: An explanation of how the evidence proves the point
review.why: Point, evidence, explain. The explanation connects the proof to the point.

review.q: Which is a transition between ideas in informative writing?
choices: By the time we got inside
review.why: On the other hand moves between ideas. The others move through time in a story.
